questions.q: What is this lesson's node-pool downsizing scenario, as the guide frames it?
options: A verified account of a specific real company's outage
A purely hypothetical exercise with no connection to real operational risk
An illustrative, clearly-fictional scenario built to show a real and common tension between cost optimization and reliability
A description of a bug in Azure's autoscaler itself
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames Ridgeline Outfitters as a scenario, not a reported incident -- illustrating a real, common tension rather than claiming a specific real-world event.

questions.q: Why did dropping the checkout node pool from six nodes to four pass review cleanly at the time?
options: It was approved by platform engineers looking at average utilization alone, with no SRE reviewer checking the SLO's headroom assumption
It required no pull request at all
The SLO was deleted before the change was approved
Terraform refused to apply the change, so it was never actually merged
questions.explain: The PR was reviewed and approved based on average CPU utilization, a legitimate right-sizing signal, but nobody on the SRE rotation for order-service was in that review loop.

questions.q: During the incident, what did the trace data from Lesson 29's instrumentation show was dominating the latency spike?
options: A database deadlock
An expired TLS certificate
Pod scheduling delay during node-pool autoscaling -- a capacity problem, not application code
A bug in the checkout service's own business logic
questions.explain: The dominant span during the breach was pod scheduling delay while the cluster scaled from four nodes back toward six -- a capacity issue, not a code defect.

questions.q: What let the postmortem connect the latency breach back to a node-pool change made three weeks earlier?
options: A guess made during the on-call page
Checking the AKS node pool's change history against the incident timestamp, prompted by the cost dashboard already showing when the spend drop took effect
The autoscaler logged the root cause directly in its alert message
Nothing connected them; the postmortem treated it only as an autoscaling-lag issue
questions.explain: The cost dashboard from Lesson 30 had logged exactly when the spend drop took effect, which is what pointed the postmortem toward checking the node pool's change history at that same timestamp.

questions.q: What corrective action does the postmortem add specifically to prevent this class of incident from recurring?
options: Disable autoscaling entirely on all node pools
Remove the checkout SLO so it can no longer be breached
Stop running any further cost-optimization reviews
Require an SRE reviewer on any node pool or instance-size change for a service with an active SLO, and add error-budget context to the right-sizing checklist
questions.explain: The fix is a process gate -- SRE review on capacity changes for SLO-bound services, plus stating the error budget and autoscaler warm-up time on the right-sizing checklist -- not disabling the tools that caught the problem.
